peers.note: Rates are per 1,000 residents for each city's principal county, because the Census Bureau publishes components of change for counties, not cities. measures.name: Share of residents born abroad
measures.definition: Share of all residents who were born outside the United States and were not U.S. citizens at birth.

source.name: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-year estimates, table B05002 (place of birth by nativity and citizenship status)

source.name: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2025 1-year estimates, table B05002, places

measures.method: Foreign born (B05002_013) divided by total population (B05002_001), times 100. People born in Puerto Rico, U.S. island areas or abroad to American parents count as native. Margins of error for the share are derived from the published margins of the two counts with the Census Bureau's formula for proportions (ACS General Handbook, chapter 8). Citywide figures are for New York city (place 3651000); peers are matched on place GEOID (state + place Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS)) from data/peers.json; borough figures are the five counties.

The 2005 ACS covered only people in households; group quarters (dorms, prisons, nursing homes, shelters) were added in 2006. 2005 values are not strictly comparable to later years.

All ACS figures are survey estimates. moe is the 90 percent margin of error, published by the Census Bureau for single cells and derived with the Bureau's approximation formulas for sums, shares and ratios.

measures.name: Share of 25- to 54-year-olds with a job
measures.definition: Share of residents aged 25 to 54 who have a job (civilian employed or in the Armed Forces).

source.name: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-year estimates, table B23001 (sex by age by employment status for the population 16 and over)
source.endpoint: https://api.census.gov/data/2025/acs/acs1 (and the same dataset for each year 2005-2025, 2020 excepted; variables B23001)

source.name: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2025 1-year estimates, table B23001, places

measures.method: Formula: prime-age employment rate = 100 x (sum over men and women, ages 25-29, 30-34, 35-44 and 45-54, of [civilian employed + in Armed Forces]) / (sum over the same eight sex-and-age groups of total population). The denominator is everyone in those age groups, including people in group quarters such as jails and nursing homes and people not in the labor force. Margins of error: sums use the root-sum-of-squares of the published cell margins, and the share uses the Census Bureau's formula for proportions. Citywide figures are for New York city (place 3651000); peers are matched on place GEOID (state + place Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS)) from data/peers.json; borough figures are the five counties.
caveats: Armed Forces members count as employed; in New York City they are a tiny share of 25- to 54-year-olds.

American Community Survey (ACS) employment status refers to the week before the survey, spread across the whole year; it is not the same concept or source as the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) household-survey employment-population ratio.

measures.name: Payroll jobs
measures.definition: Jobs on employer payrolls located in New York City (all five boroughs), total nonfarm, annual average of monthly counts, in thousands, not seasonally adjusted.

latest_extra.note: Monthly count in thousands, not seasonally adjusted; compare with the same month a year earlier, not with the annual average. Preliminary.

source.name: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (State and Metro Area), New York City, total nonfarm, not seasonally adjusted, series SMU36935610000000001

measures.method: Annual value = mean of the 12 monthly not-seasonally-adjusted CES employment levels for the calendar year (thousands of jobs), rounded to one decimal. Monthly values come from the keyless BLS v1 API, which does not return annual averages.

Peers left out: CES publishes this city-level definition for New York City, but for most of the 25 peer cities it publishes only metropolitan-area or county figures, so there is no same-geography comparison.

measures.name: Average hourly earnings after inflation
measures.definition: Average hourly earnings of all private-sector employees on New York City payrolls, annual average, in 2025 dollars (deflated with the New York-area consumer price index).

latest_extra.note: Monthly figure in current (nominal) dollars, not adjusted for inflation and not seasonally adjusted, so it is not directly comparable to the 2025-dollar annual series. Preliminary.

source.name: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Employment Statistics (State and Metro Area), New York City, total private, average hourly earnings of all employees, not seasonally adjusted, series SMU36935610500000003

deflator_source.name: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), New York-Newark-Jersey City, all items, not seasonally adjusted, series CUURS12ASA0

measures.method: AHE_y = mean of the 12 monthly CES average-hourly-earnings values for year y. CPI_y = mean of the monthly Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) values (CUURS12ASA0) for year y. Real value in 2025 dollars = AHE_y x CPI_2025 / CPI_y, rounded to cents. Peers left out: Current Employment Statistics (CES) earnings series at the city level exist for New York City but not for most peer cities.

measures.name: Subway and bus ridership
measures.definition: Annual Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) subway ridership plus MTA New York City Transit and MTA Bus Company bus ridership, in millions of trips.

latest_extra.note: Subway plus bus trips so far this year, from the MTA daily ridership dataset; compares with 1,497.2 million trips on the same dates of 2025, up 0.4 percent.

source.name: MTA, 'Subway and bus ridership for 2019' page (2014-2018) and MTA Monthly Ridership & Traffic Data (data.ny.gov xfre-bxip, 2019 on)

measures.method: Annual subway ridership plus New York City Transit bus plus MTA Bus Company ridership. 2014-2018 are the annual totals in the three summary tables on MTA's 2019 ridership page; 2019-2025 are sums of the twelve monthly values for agencies 'Subway', 'NYCT Bus' and 'MTA Bus' in the MTA monthly dataset (years with fewer than 12 months are left out). The two sources agree on 2019 (checked within 0.5%). 2025 was 72.6% of 2019. latest_extra compares the sum of daily Subway and Bus counts from 1 January through the dataset's latest date (2026-11-12) with the same dates a year earlier.
caveats: Staten Island Railway, commuter rail and paratransit are excluded.

The MTA daily dataset (sayj-mze2) starts on 1 March 2020, so it cannot give full-year 2020; the monthly dataset is used for every year from 2019 so the series has one consistent source. Annual sums of the daily data differ from the monthly totals by: 2021 subway -0.0%, bus -0.4%; 2022 subway -0.1%, bus -0.4%; 2023 subway -0.2%, bus -0.3%; 2024 subway -0.1%, bus -0.0%; 2025 subway +0.0%, bus -0.8%.
Pre-2014 annual totals were not used: the MTA pages carrying them could not be retrieved.
2020-2022 reflect the pandemic collapse and recovery.

The peer comparison is left out. The National Transit Database puts New York ridership in 2025 at 87.5 percent of 2019, but the Metropolitan Transportation Authority's own counts put it at 72.6 percent, mostly because the two count bus riders differently, so New York could not be ranked fairly.

measures.name: Average bus speed
measures.definition: Average speed of Metropolitan Transportation Authority (MTA) local, limited, Select Bus Service and express buses in New York City, in miles per hour: total bus miles divided by total operating hours across all routes and months.

latest_extra.note: Same calculation for January-October; January-October 2025 was 8.31 mph.

source.name: MTA Bus Speeds (data.ny.gov cudb-vcni, 'MTA Bus Speeds: Beginning 2015')

measures.method: For each calendar year with all 12 months: sum of total_mileage divided by sum of total_operating_time over every route, borough, trip type (local/limited, Select Bus Service, express), day type and peak/off-peak period. This weights each route-month by its operating hours (equivalently, it is total bus miles over total bus hours), rather than averaging route speeds. The borough breakdown applies the same formula within each borough.
caveats: The dataset is titled 'Beginning 2015' but its rows start in January 2019, so there is no earlier history from this source.
The dataset's column descriptions for mileage and operating time are swapped; the values (and the dataset's own average_speed field) confirm mileage divided by hours gives mph.

measures.name: Average commute time
measures.definition: Average one-way travel time to work, in minutes, for workers 16 and over who do not work from home.

source.name: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 1-year estimates, tables B08013 (aggregate travel time to work) and B08134 (workers who did not work from home, by travel time)
source.endpoint: https://api.census.gov/data/2025/acs/acs1 (and the same dataset for each year 2005-2025, 2020 excepted; variables B08013, B08134)

source.name: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2025 1-year estimates, table B08013, B08134, places

measures.method: Mean travel time = aggregate travel time to work in minutes (B08013_001) / workers 16 and over who did not work from home (B08134_001). This reproduces the Census Bureau's published 'mean travel time to work' (table S0801). Margin of error from the published margins with the Census Bureau's formula for ratios. Citywide figures are for New York city (place 3651000); peers are matched on place GEOID (state + place Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS)) from data/peers.json; borough figures are the five counties.
caveats: People who work from home are excluded. Remote work rose sharply after 2019, so the mix of people who commute changed; 2021 onward is not strictly comparable to earlier years.
Travel time is self-reported for the week before the survey, door to door, one way.

The American Community Survey (ACS) 1-year 2020 standard tables were never released (the Census Bureau published only experimental estimates because of pandemic data-collection problems), so 2020 is missing from every ACS series.
The 2005 ACS covered only people in households; group quarters (dorms, prisons, nursing homes, shelters) were added in 2006. 2005 values are not strictly comparable to later years.

All ACS figures are survey estimates. moe is the 90 percent margin of error, published by the Census Bureau for single cells and derived with the Bureau's approximation formulas for sums, shares and ratios.

Margins of error: for 2010, 2011, 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 the moe is the one the Census Bureau publishes in subject table S0801 (which matches this estimate to its published rounding) for the city, the 2025 peers and the boroughs. Other years, and the race breakdowns, use the derived margin described in the method.

measures.status_reason: The indicator ended after fiscal 2023: the fiscal 2023 Mayor's Management Report (MMR) removed it while the Scorecard inspection program is overhauled, and no fiscal 2024-fiscal 2026 values exist. fiscal 2019 has no rating (MMR prints NA).

measures.name: Turnout in mayoral general elections
measures.definition: Votes cast for mayor in the November general election as a share of the city's citizen voting-age population (U.S. citizens 18 and older) that year.

source.name: New York City Board of Elections certified Statement and Return reports, Mayor (citywide recap), general elections 2005-2025; Census Bureau ACS 1-year estimates

measures.method: Turnout = votes recorded for mayor / citizen voting-age population x 100. Votes recorded for mayor are the Board of Elections' certified 'Total Votes' for the office (all candidates and write-ins; ballots left blank or overvoted for mayor, shown as 'Unrecorded', are excluded). The denominator is American Community Survey (ACS) 1-year table B29001 (citizen voting-age population) for New York city for the same year; B29001 is not published for 2005-2013, so for those years it is built from table B05003 as people 18+ minus non-citizens 18+ (male B05003_008-B05003_012 plus female B05003_019-B05003_023), which reproduces B29001 exactly in 2017 (checked). Borough breakdown uses the county recap totals over county B29001. Figures: 2005: 1,289,935 votes for mayor (1,315,360 ballots) / 4,716,299 CVAP (ACS 1-year B05003); 2009: 1,154,802 votes for mayor (1,178,057 ballots) / 5,159,802 CVAP (ACS 1-year B05003); 2013: 1,087,710 votes for mayor (1,102,400 ballots) / 5,294,114 CVAP (ACS 1-year B05003); 2017: 1,148,665 votes for mayor (1,166,314 ballots) / 5,530,640 CVAP (ACS 1-year B29001, margin of error (MOE) +/-21,106); 2021: 1,125,258 votes for mayor (1,149,172 ballots) / 5,546,959 CVAP (ACS 1-year B29001, MOE +/-27,010); 2025: 2,194,204 votes for mayor (2,218,647 ballots) / 5,814,406 CVAP (ACS 1-year B29001, MOE +/-30,278).
caveats: The denominator is a survey estimate with a margin of error; turnout margins of error are not published and are not computed here.
Total ballots cast (including ballots with no vote for mayor) run about 1-2 percent higher than votes for mayor; the figures are in method.
The citizen voting-age population (CVAP) counts all adult citizens, including those not registered, so this is lower than turnout of registered voters.

measures.name: City debt per resident
measures.definition: Total outstanding debt of New York City's primary government (general obligation bonds, Transitional Finance Authority and other city-backed debt, plus lease and other obligations), per resident, at fiscal year end, as reported in the Comptroller's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, adjusted for inflation to 2025 dollars with the New York-area consumer price index.

source.name: New York City Comptroller, Annual Comprehensive Financial Report, Part III Statistical Information, 'Ratios of Outstanding Debt by Type-Ten Year Trend'

peers.note: Different source and definition from the New York City series: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy Fiscally Standardized Cities (FiSC), total debt outstanding per resident in 2023 (Census of Governments data). FiSC states values in 2023 dollars (its Consumer Price Index (CPI) factor is 1 that year); they are moved to 2025 dollars here with the same New York-area Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) as the New York City series (2025 annual average / 2023 annual average = 1.0730). FiSC adds the shares of county, school district and special district debt that serve each city's residents, which adjusts for New York's roles as city, county and school district. Not in FiSC: Fort Worth.

source.name: Lincoln Institute of Land Policy, Fiscally Standardized Cities database (full dataset)

measures.method: The 'Per Capita' column of the ten-year table in two ACFRs: fiscal 2007-fiscal 2016: Comptroller's Comprehensive Annual Financial Report (CAFR) for Fiscal 2016, 'Ratios of Outstanding Debt by Type-Ten Year Trend', printed page 378 (PDF page 407), https://comptroller.nyc.gov/wp-content/uploads/documents/CAFR2016.pdf; fiscal 2017-fiscal 2026: Comptroller's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR) for Fiscal 2026, 'Ratios of Outstanding Debt by Type-Ten Year Trend', printed page 463 (PDF page 497), https://comptroller.nyc.gov/wp-content/uploads/documents/ACFR-2026.pdf. Per capita is the Comptroller's figure: total primary government debt divided by the prior year's city population (table footnote 4). Each fiscal year's nominal figure is converted to 2025 dollars by multiplying by the ratio of the 2025 annual-average New York-Newark-Jersey City CPI-U (BLS CUURS12ASA0, not seasonally adjusted, 345.511) to the average of that index over the fiscal year (July of the prior year through June), from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) public API. fiscal 2026 averages 11 months because BLS published no value for October 2025 (Data unavailable due to the 2025 lapse in appropriations). The nominal figures are in nominal_series and the fiscal-year index values in deflator.
caveats: Lease obligations rose sharply in fiscal 2022 when the City implemented Governmental Accounting Standards Board (GASB) Statement 87 (ACFR fiscal 2026 table footnote 5), so much of the fiscal 2021-fiscal 2022 jump (from $11,960 to $13,931 per resident in nominal dollars) is an accounting change, not new borrowing.

Values are in 2025 dollars using the New York-area consumer price index, a measure of household prices, not of the costs the City borrows for; the Comptroller's nominal figures are kept in nominal_series.
New York's debt covers functions that elsewhere belong to counties, school districts and some state agencies, so per-resident city debt is not directly comparable with other city governments.

measures.name: State and local taxes on a typical family
measures.definition: Estimated state and local income, property, sales and auto taxes paid by a hypothetical family of three earning $75,000 a year in New York City, as a percent of income, from the D.C. Chief Financial Officer's annual nationwide comparison of the largest city in each state.

source.name: Government of the District of Columbia, Office of the Chief Financial Officer (Office of Revenue Analysis), 'Tax Rates and Tax Burdens in the District of Columbia: A Nationwide Comparison', editions 2008-2023

peers.note: Same report and income level. The report covers only the largest city in each state, so San Antonio, San Diego, Dallas, Fort Worth, Austin, San Jose, San Francisco, El Paso are not in it.

source.name: Government of the District of Columbia, Office of the Chief Financial Officer, 2023 Tax Rates and Tax Burdens in the District of Columbia: A Nationwide Comparison, Table 1c (PDF page 27)

measures.method: From each edition's table of estimated burdens of major taxes for a hypothetical family earning $75,000 (Table 1c in recent editions), the New York City row's total burden as a percent of income (income + property + sales + auto taxes). $75,000 is used because it is the income level the report uses for its headline maps of total, income, property and sales tax burdens, and it appears in every edition. Pages: 2008 edition PDF page 19 ($7,337 total); 2009 edition PDF page 19 ($8,173 total); 2010 edition PDF page 18 ($7,833 total); 2012 edition PDF page 18 ($8,692 total); 2013 edition PDF page 18 ($8,728 total); 2014 edition PDF page 25 ($8,293 total); 2015 edition PDF page 25 ($7,840 total); 2016 edition PDF page 26 ($8,871 total); 2017 edition PDF page 26 ($8,657 total); 2018 edition PDF page 26 ($8,785 total); 2019 edition PDF page 28 ($8,586 total); 2020 edition PDF page 28 ($8,621 total); 2021 edition PDF page 27 ($8,719 total); 2022 edition PDF page 27 ($7,494 total); 2023 edition PDF page 27 ($8,431 total).
caveats: The report itself advises readers not to compare its hypothetical burdens across years, because small changes in its assumptions can make such comparisons misleading (2023 edition, PDF page 11); treat the series as a sequence of single-year comparisons across cities, not a trend.
Editions cover taxes in effect through December 31 of the edition year; the latest edition found is 2023. No 2011 edition was found, so 2011 is missing.

The report assumes the family owns its home at this income level (only the $25,000 family is assumed to rent), so the property tax figure depends on the report's housing-value assumption for each city.
